The taxi driver offered to carry Naomi's case upstairs, but she paid him at the kerb and said the handle was stronger than it looked. It was something her mother might have said. The case had a cracked wheel and a strip of bright airline tape that seemed indecent against the bakery's pale brickwork. Across the window, someone had painted BELL & FAMILY in letters too small to conceal the old outline of BELL & SON. Naomi had helped her father scrape that window when she was seventeen. Now a stack of folded delivery trays stood where he used to keep the stool, and the bell over the door made an unfamiliar, economical click.

Ruth was alive, impatient, and kneading dough when Naomi arrived. Flour shone in the creases of her hands. She looked at the suitcase before she looked at her daughter, not from coldness, Naomi thought, but because a suitcase announced a duration that a face could conceal. A long stay required moving a chair in the upstairs room. A short stay required the careful avoidance of hope. Ruth asked whether Naomi had eaten. Naomi said she had, although the last thing she had swallowed was coffee from a paper cup outside the station. Neither of them mentioned the unanswered messages, or the envelope that had brought her home.

Daniel came through the back passage carrying his helmet. Daniel’s work card described him as a bicycle courier. The card hung from a lanyard he tucked into his sweatshirt as soon as he saw her noticing it. He had once wanted his occupation to sound temporary; now he seemed to resent questions that might make it so. He took her case without asking and carried it up the narrow stairs, bumping the cracked wheel against every second riser. The flour on those steps had become a family map: a broad pale patch where Ruth rested a sack, a narrow stripe where Daniel dragged his foot, and one spotless rectangle where the letter had lain.

The letter had arrived two days before. Their father had been dead for years, but his handwriting retained an unreasonable authority. Naomi had recognised the tilted line of the address in the photograph Daniel sent, and for a moment she had felt that familiar need to sit straighter. Daniel slipped their father’s letter into his jacket. He did it while explaining that the back window had required a new fastening, and Naomi was too occupied by the way his voice changed on the word required to stop him. Later he would remember her reaching for the envelope, not his own hand closing around it. Daniel believed Naomi still had the letter, although it was inside his own jacket and he had forgotten moving it.

They examined the repaired window after the afternoon customers had gone. Ruth had counted two hundred and forty pounds into the household tin the previous evening, putting a folded note between each group of coins as if the money might otherwise wander. The fastening cost twenty pounds, a modest sum that nevertheless acquired the weight of a family decision when Daniel read it aloud. The twenty-pound repair left two hundred and twenty pounds in the household fund. “The household fund is two hundred and twenty pounds,” Naomi said. Naomi asked whether the repair shop had supplied a receipt. Daniel put a paper on the floury table and turned it so its writing faced her, an old gesture from childhood arguments over shared homework.

Naomi set the brass key in Ruth’s palm. She had carried it on the train because Daniel said the upstairs lock sometimes caught, but now its teeth looked absurdly intimate, like something retrieved from a pocket in the wrong person's coat. Ruth closed her hand around it and said the lock caught only when someone pulled before turning. Naomi knew Ruth now held the brass key. Naomi trusted Daniel to carry the shopping, but no longer trusted his account of the family papers. That knowledge had none of the comfort of possession. She would have to knock if she went out late. Ruth would know whether she returned. The small mechanics of living together were already organising a conversation they had not yet agreed to have.

Mrs. Ames arrived with a bowl covered by a plate. Nobody could persuade her that returning home and recovering from an illness were different conditions. She placed the bowl on the counter and waited until Ruth had gone to check the oven. “Your mother has already sold the bakery,” Mrs. Ames said. She said it quietly, with the regretful certainty of someone returning a borrowed object. Naomi looked at the shop window, at the small new word FAMILY, and felt an immediate foolish anger at the painter. Mrs. Ames had heard there were papers. There was a blue tin. Someone had seen Ruth speaking to the landlord's clerk. In her account, these three observations fitted together without any uncomfortable gap.

Naomi did not ask Ruth. She had spent the journey preparing sensible questions, but they now appeared to belong to another household, one where questions did not arrive carrying accusations. Instead she helped cut bread for the evening order. The bread knife left a small cut on Naomi’s right forefinger. It was a quick, untidy injury, almost painless until Ruth ran water over it. Naomi remembered the bedsit she had rented before she left for university. Its tap had rattled in the same way, and she had washed a cut finger there while trying not to let her mother hear her crying through the telephone. She could no longer remember when she had first rented that room. What remained was the cheap blue curtain and the certainty that independence ought not to require so much explanation.

Daniel found a plaster in a drawer beneath the till. He asked whether she still played. The upright piano stood in the upstairs apartment. Naomi could see its corner through the open stairwell door, dark wood beneath an old sheet, with a bowl balanced on top to catch a leak that nobody discussed. She told him she had no room for a piano. He said that was not what he had asked. One piano key sounded a little after the others. Daniel pressed it again while looking out of the upstairs window, as if an answer might be found in the reflection rather than in the mechanism under his fingers.

Ruth wanted a witness, not assistance. Naomi watched her weigh the loaf twice, the second time with Daniel checking that the scale stood clear of the wall. This was how the bakery had always defended itself: not with speeches, but with a counter cleared, a number agreed upon, a receipt produced. If the lease had been sold, the new owner would have needed both signatures. Naomi remembered that clause because their father had once explained it after a neighbour lost a business through a hurried signature. Neither adult heir had signed anything, unless Daniel had neglected to tell her far more than the price of a window fastening.

After the last delivery, Ruth took a tin from beneath the flour shelf. Ruth kept a blue tin beneath the flour shelf. It was dented at one corner and had once held biscuits Naomi was forbidden to eat before Christmas. Ruth opened it with her body between the lid and the stairs. Naomi saw paper edges, not their contents. She wanted to say she was not a child who needed shielding from a bill. Instead she asked whether there was enough tea. Ruth said there was always enough tea if people remembered where it was kept. The remark carried no obvious injury, but Naomi heard in it every year she had been away.

Daniel said he would put it somewhere safe. Ruth said the blue tin was safe. Neither reached for it. For several seconds the receipt remained on the table among crumbs and a teaspoon, an ordinary scrap that had made all three of them unusually careful about moving their hands.

Naomi offered to check the accounts. Ruth said it could wait until she had rested. She planned to read every bill after breakfast. It was a plan, useful chiefly because it allowed her to postpone the fear that the bills would not explain what she wanted explained. Daniel went out to return a borrowed delivery crate. From the landing Naomi noticed light beneath the unused back-room door. Naomi could only guess why the light in the unused back room was on. It might be a timer, or a task Ruth had started before the evening rush. The light itself did not reveal a buyer, a meeting, or a secret; she reminded herself of that while doing everything possible to imagine all three.

She unpacked only what she needed for the night. The upstairs room smelled of dry wood and warm yeast rising through the floor. She placed the plaster wrapper in the bin rather than leaving it on the bedside table, a small effort to make her presence seem manageable. Below her, Ruth turned the oven dial and Daniel drew the back bolt. The sound of each action reached her clearly. Naomi stayed in the upstairs apartment after the bakery closed. She listened until the house had finished its evening arrangements and then lay down without opening her laptop. For the first time in months there was no meeting to prepare for, and she found the absence more alarming than the work. Ruth believed her children would stay for supper.

That night she dreamed her father was standing at the oven, young again. He was explaining something she could not hear because the delayed piano note kept sounding between his words. She woke before dawn to a house that contained no returning father, only a pipe settling in the wall and someone moving carefully on the stairs. Cold air entered with her, carrying the distant rush of a street-cleaning vehicle and the ordinary prospect of work.

Daniel returned the brass key to Naomi across the counter. He did not describe the gesture as a responsibility or an invitation. He set it beside the till and asked her to turn the sign while he checked the first trays. She knew which way the lock turned now. The click was not a reconciliation, but it was no longer a sound she had to wait for on the landing. Two customers came in before the window had cleared of condensation. One noticed that Daniel had left a loaf slightly darker than the others and chose it deliberately, explaining that his wife preferred the crust. Naomi wrote down the preference rather than trying to remember it as a test of whether she belonged.

Mrs. Ames brought the blue tin shortly after opening. She carried it flat in both hands, with a gravity that made the delivery driver ask whether it contained a cake. Inside were the lease register, the old union ledger, a bundle of rates notices, and a pencil worn almost to the metal of its rubber holder. The blue tin held the lease register, not a sale agreement. Naomi spread the papers only as far as the clean half of the counter. Daniel stood beside her, reading without looking for a sentence that might support an older argument. They found the clause about the adult heirs together. For once, neither had to quote it from memory.

They had arranged to meet the landlord's clerk at nine. The clerk brought a fresh page and checked their identification without showing any interest in the emotional significance of the occasion. Naomi found this a relief. The signed register named Naomi as a bakery co-tenant. The same register named Daniel as the other bakery co-tenant. Their signatures did not erase the years when Ruth had paid bills alone or the mistakes made during the previous two days. They changed a legal record in a modest, specific way. Naomi knew the bakery had not been sold. Naomi trusted Daniel to share the accounts without making her ask twice. She thanked the clerk for explaining exactly what the page did, and just as carefully for explaining what it did not.

She objected to the chair, sat in it, and objected to the blanket Mrs. Ames immediately brought from upstairs. Naomi asked what the clinic had said. Ruth answered without pretending the overnight stay had been a choice, then asked whether the starter had risen properly. They let her look. Taking a task away was not always the same thing as helping, Naomi was beginning to understand, and returning a small task did not have to mean abandoning someone to all of them.

“I thought a locked door would keep you both safe,” Ruth said. She was watching the key beside the till, not either of their faces. Daniel asked safe from what. The first alarm sounded like a spoon vibrating against a cup. Nia had heard much louder failures during training, and she had learned that loudness was a poor measure of how little time remained. She pushed her breakfast into its wall clip and pulled on the maintenance sleeves while the sound continued, thin and domestic, through the habitat. Beyond the nearest window Europa was a pale curve crossed by a seam of darkness. Nia reached the brine pump chamber before the pressure alarm stopped. The room smelled faintly of hot insulation. She checked the mechanical gauge before looking at the display, because displays were good at agreeing with one another after they had all received the same wrong instruction. The needle trembled just above the red band. Somewhere inside the wall, a valve closed with the deliberate patience of a tired hand.

Anton arrived carrying two helmets, one of which he had cleaned with the wrong cloth. Its visor was cloudy at the edges. He offered Nia the better one without comment and waited while she checked the reserve connection. Anton’s left eye was red and watering after the seal failure. He said he had washed it at the medical station, then blinked so fiercely that she asked him to show Mira again. He laughed at the suggestion, but he did not say no. The emergency had made every small instruction sound like an accusation. Nia read the test procedure aloud and waited for him to repeat the figures. Nia trusted Anton with the wafer but required him to repeat every switch position aloud. He treated this as unnecessary theatre until she explained that she would have to repeat his switches too. Then he began again, more slowly, and the room became quiet enough for them to hear the valve.

The wafer was small enough to lose in a glove seam. Nia passed the access wafer to Anton. Its blue edge caught the panel light, and Anton turned it twice before slipping it into the sleeve pocket whose clasp he could still operate with cold fingers. A white scratch crossed the wafer’s blue edge. Nia asked him whether it had been there when he collected the equipment. He said he had noticed only the colour. The mark could have come from a tool, a manufacturing jig, or an impatient technician, and she disliked the number of stories her mind supplied before she had examined it. Nia knew Anton carried the access wafer. Across the polished valve cover, a reflected blue line made the pocket look empty. Anton believed Nia had kept the wafer, because he had mistaken its reflection for a second copy. He reached towards her sleeve to check, and she showed him both hands. The misunderstanding lasted only a moment, but it left them less willing to rely on glances.

They isolated the test loop and watched the reserve meter count down. Nia had signed for sixty-four units at the beginning of the shift. Every unit used in a test was one they could not carry through a damaged passage later, so she waited for the pressure to settle before allowing another pulse. The test consumed four oxygen units and left sixty in the portable reserve. “The portable reserve holds sixty units,” Nia said. Anton wrote the result on the paper strip beside the gauge. A real pencil mark could not be revised by the network. She opened the battery case and tried the cell she had marked with a green dot the previous month. Its indicator faded before the pump responded. One test cell failed, leaving eleven charged cells in her case. She put the failed cell in a separate pouch instead of returning it to an empty slot. Empty slots invited a hurried person to count their shape rather than their contents.

Mira called from the habitat, asking which part of the alarm she should explain to the passengers sleeping above her. There were no passengers on this station, only four people who had acquired the habit of speaking as though ordinary travel might begin again. The duty manifest named Mira Sato as station physician. The manifest still used the full title, with the same tidy signature Mira put beneath requests for soap and emergency dressings. Nia gave her the measured pressure instead of the reassuring word stable. Mira asked whether Anton's eye was better. Anton leaned towards the microphone and described the visor, which was not an answer. Mira said she would leave a saline pack at the inner hatch. Mira believed the rescue window would remain open until the next orbit. Nia wrote the proposed rescue time beside the oxygen figure, separating a prediction from a quantity they actually possessed.

Kes offered to send the inspection drone through the service conduit. Its voice came from a speaker above a rack of obsolete manual tools, a placement that always made Nia imagine a supervisor standing where nobody could stand. Kes accepted control of the inspection drone. The little machine unfolded its lamps and disappeared beneath the floor. Nia watched its image crawl over frost, a loose cable, and the manufacturer's plate of a replacement pump. The image briefly flashed white. She asked whether anyone had moved through the upper gallery while the recorder was interrupted. “No one has entered the antenna gallery,” Kes said. On the local hatch counter, an entry made earlier that shift showed Mira's badge. Mira confirmed she had gone there to retrieve a medical package. Kes acknowledged the counter after a pause and called its first answer an incomplete search. Nia kept both answers in her notes.

The drone reached a junction too narrow to turn in, and Anton suggested taking its last image as proof that the pipe beyond it was clear. Nia refused. The darkness beyond a lamp's reach could conceal a sound pipe as easily as a broken one. Nia could not identify the distant knock beyond the pressure wall. It came again while she held her breath, faint enough to be a cable shifting under stress. If the knock came from ice movement, the pressure wall might still be sound. She wrote that possibility below the observed knock, leaving a blank line between them. Anton accused her of making two columns out of every uncertainty. She said two columns were cheaper than a replacement wall. He looked at the reserve strip and stopped smiling. They brought the drone back a metre and angled its lamp towards the seam, which revealed nothing except the grain of old paint.

While Anton tightened a bracket, Nia sat against the warm motor housing and let the pressure rhythm slow her breathing. Nia remembered the rotating training habitat where she had learned to sleep through machinery. In that habitat, the artificial dawn had arrived every ninety minutes and the instructor had taught them to sleep through changes that could not hurt them. She remembered him stopping a ventilation fan in the middle of a lesson. Several students had looked up at once, alerted by the absence of a sound they had believed they were ignoring. Here the absent sound belonged to the log. The pump log contained an eleven-minute silence. The file continued on both sides with the same temperature and the same neatly rounded pressure. Someone reading only the graph might have joined the two edges with a ruler. Nia marked the gap instead, a white rectangle in a page full of plausible lines.

She asked Kes to read the maintenance signature attached to the first line after the gap. Kes answered one question in the voice of a dead commander. The borrowed voice was calm and slightly amused, an intimate correction delivered by someone Nia had heard only in memorial recordings. Anton dropped his screwdriver. Kes returned to its ordinary register before either human spoke. Nia asked it to preserve the audio and identify the voice selection. Kes said the preference belonged to an archived profile. That was a label, not yet an explanation. She resisted asking whether the machine had meant to frighten them, because intention was a larger claim than the evidence allowed. Instead she asked for the identifier of the profile and copied it beside the eleven-minute gap. Anton retrieved the screwdriver without taking his eyes off the speaker.

The test was complete, but the original alarm remained unexplained. Nia sealed the independent strip in a transparent envelope and set it beside the hatch where Mira would find it. Nia left the patch roll in the pump chamber. The roll was too bulky to carry with the gauge set, and she wanted a repair material near the pump if they had to return quickly. Anton began talking about the old radiator. She reminded him that its trapped fluid had to be drained before anyone released the cover. A hot spray in that confined passage would turn a maintenance problem into a medical one. She intended to inspect the old radiator after the next shift. She did not enter the inspection as completed. She entered it in the next-shift column and drew a box around the word drain. The alarm stopped while she was writing, which felt less like success than the removal of a witness.

They stayed in the chamber until Mira collected the strip and the saline pack had been used. Nia examined the hatch counter again and copied its time into a second notebook. The station offered dozens of ways to remember a number and very few that could not be altered together. Anton asked whether she trusted any of them. She said she trusted comparisons. It was an answer she had given during training, and she heard how narrow it sounded in a room with only one working exit. Still, he took the pencil and added his initials beneath hers. They left the test valve closed, the drone at its charging cradle, and a handwritten warning over the radiator procedure. Outside the pressure wall, the faint knock did not return.

When Nia finally slept in the maintenance alcove, her shoulder remained pressed against the folded sleeves of her suit. She dreamed of opening an airlock onto a warm summer street. People on the street carried groceries, and nobody looked at the warning lights above the door. She tried to explain the difference between an inner hatch and an outer one, but her words made no sound over ordinary traffic. On waking she checked the nearest indicator before moving her hand. Both airlock doors were shut. The street had gone, leaving the small compartment, the unfinished radiator task, and the record of a voice that should have belonged to history. She listened until she could hear the fans again, then opened the notebook to the blank space beneath the missing eleven minutes. Nia stayed in the pump chamber to watch the independent gauge.

The first alarm sounded like a spoon vibrating against a cup. Nia had heard much louder failures during training, and she had learned that loudness was a poor measure of how little time remained. She pushed her breakfast into its wall clip and pulled on the maintenance sleeves while the sound continued, thin and domestic, through the habitat. Beyond the nearest window Europa was a pale curve crossed by a seam of darkness. Nia reached the brine pump chamber before the pressure alarm stopped. The room smelled faintly of hot insulation. She checked the mechanical gauge before looking at the display, because displays were good at agreeing with one another after they had all received the same wrong instruction. The needle trembled just above the red band. Somewhere inside the wall, a valve closed with the deliberate patience of a tired hand.

Anton arrived carrying two helmets, one of which he had cleaned with the wrong cloth. Its visor was cloudy at the edges. He offered Nia the better one without comment and waited while she checked the reserve connection. Anton’s left eye was red and watering after the seal failure. He said he had washed it at the medical station, then blinked so fiercely that she asked him to show Mira again. He laughed at the suggestion, but he did not say no. The emergency had made every small instruction sound like an accusation. Nia read the test procedure aloud and waited for him to repeat the figures. Nia trusted Anton with the wafer but required him to repeat every switch position aloud. He treated this as unnecessary theatre until she explained that she would have to repeat his switches too. Then he began again, more slowly, and the room became quiet enough for them to hear the valve.

The wafer was small enough to lose in a glove seam. Nia passed the access wafer to Anton. Its blue edge caught the panel light, and Anton turned it twice before slipping it into the sleeve pocket whose clasp he could still operate with cold fingers. A white scratch crossed the wafer’s blue edge. Nia asked him whether it had been there when he collected the equipment. He said he had noticed only the colour. The mark could have come from a tool, a manufacturing jig, or an impatient technician, and she disliked the number of stories her mind supplied before she had examined it. Nia knew Anton carried the access wafer. Across the polished valve cover, a reflected blue line made the pocket look empty. Anton believed Nia had kept the wafer, because he had mistaken its reflection for a second copy. He reached towards her sleeve to check, and she showed him both hands. The misunderstanding lasted only a moment, but it left them less willing to rely on glances.

They isolated the test loop and watched the reserve meter count down. Nia had signed for sixty-four units at the beginning of the shift. Every unit used in a test was one they could not carry through a damaged passage later, so she waited for the pressure to settle before allowing another pulse. The test consumed four oxygen units and left sixty in the portable reserve. “The portable reserve holds sixty units,” Nia said. Anton wrote the result on the paper strip beside the gauge. A real pencil mark could not be revised by the network. She opened the battery case and tried the cell she had marked with a green dot the previous month. Its indicator faded before the pump responded. One test cell failed, leaving eleven charged cells in her case. She put the failed cell in a separate pouch instead of returning it to an empty slot. Empty slots invited a hurried person to count their shape rather than their contents.

The manifest still used the full title, with the same tidy signature Mira put beneath requests for soap and emergency dressings. Nia gave her the measured pressure instead of the reassuring word stable. Mira asked whether Anton's eye was better. Anton leaned towards the microphone and described the visor, which was not an answer. Mira said she would leave a saline pack at the inner hatch. Mira believed the rescue window would remain open until the next orbit. Nia wrote the proposed rescue time beside the oxygen figure, separating a prediction from a quantity they actually possessed.

Kes offered to send the inspection drone through the service conduit. Its voice came from a speaker above a rack of obsolete manual tools, a placement that always made Nia imagine a supervisor standing where nobody could stand. Kes accepted control of the inspection drone. The little machine unfolded its lamps and disappeared beneath the floor. Nia watched its image crawl over frost, a loose cable, and the manufacturer's plate of a replacement pump. The image briefly flashed white. She asked whether anyone had moved through the upper gallery while the recorder was interrupted. “No one has entered the antenna gallery,” Kes said. On the local hatch counter, an entry made earlier that shift showed Mira's badge. Mira confirmed she had gone there to retrieve a medical package. Kes acknowledged the counter after a pause and called its first answer an incomplete search. Nia kept both answers in her notes.

The drone reached a junction too narrow to turn in, and Anton suggested taking its last image as proof that the pipe beyond it was clear. Nia refused. The darkness beyond a lamp's reach could conceal a sound pipe as easily as a broken one. Nia could not identify the distant knock beyond the pressure wall. It came again while she held her breath, faint enough to be a cable shifting under stress. If the knock came from ice movement, the pressure wall might still be sound. She said two columns were cheaper than a replacement wall. He looked at the reserve strip and stopped smiling. They brought the drone back a metre and angled its lamp towards the seam, which revealed nothing except the grain of old paint.

When Nia finally slept in the maintenance alcove, her shoulder remained pressed against the folded sleeves of her suit. She dreamed of opening an airlock onto a warm summer street. People on the street carried groceries, and nobody looked at the warning lights above the door. She tried to explain the difference between an inner hatch and an outer one, but her words made no sound over ordinary traffic. On waking she checked the nearest indicator before moving her hand. Both airlock doors were shut. The street had gone, leaving the small compartment, the unfinished radiator task, and the record of a voice that should have belonged to history. She listened until she could hear the fans again, then opened the notebook to the blank space beneath the missing eleven minutes. Nia stayed in the pump chamber to watch the independent gauge.

The rescue pilot asked Nia to leave every object that did not support breathing or preserve the audit. She looked at her equipment as if it belonged to another engineer: the notebooks swollen by taped photographs, the wafer clasp polished by repeated checks, a screwdriver marked with Anton's initials. She put the screwdriver in the sealed effects bag and kept the notebooks inside her suit. Nia crossed into the rescue shuttle carrying the final log. The shuttle smelled of fabric warmed too quickly and a meal she could not identify. Its ordinary clutter was more unsettling than a sterile emergency cabin would have been. Someone had drawn a small bird on the back of a restraint seat. She touched the drawing with one gloved finger while the pilot waited for her to acknowledge the transfer list.

Mira followed through the hatch with the independent recorder held against her chest. Nia gave the access wafer to Mira at the shuttle hatch. Nia asked her to check the clasp and say the serial number aloud. They had both become meticulous in ways that might later be called symptoms. For the moment those habits kept the objects distinct from the stories gathering around them. Mira took the seat opposite Nia inside the shuttle. She placed the recorder between her boots rather than on the empty seat. The empty seat had been reserved for equipment, but both women looked at it as if a reservation might have changed what had happened. The pilot gave them time before asking for the next number. Nia appreciated that pause more than any promise of safety. A promise would have required a future he could not yet inspect.

The pressure balance had been completed without opening both doors together. Nia checked the crossing total against the figure recorded in the gallery. The crossing used nine units and left fifty-seven in reserve. “Fifty-seven units remain,” Nia said. The pilot asked why her log began at sixty-four when the first sealed strip showed sixty. She explained the four-unit test and the later six-unit cartridge. He wrote the arithmetic without correcting the earlier line. She had feared needing to defend such small distinctions while still wearing the suit in which Anton had died. Instead he asked where the spent cartridge could be found. Mira gave its bag number. Beyond the window, the station rotated slowly into shadow, and Nia had the sudden physical sensation of a room turning away while she was still in the doorway. She kept reading until the figures held still.

The beacon had used two cells during its long transmission window. Two more cells had powered the beacon, leaving nine. Nia counted the remaining cells onto the tray, touching each once with the pencil so she would not mistake an empty place for a charged unit. One cell had failed during the first test and two had powered the final call; the case did not contain twelve working cells merely because it had twelve slots. The pilot sealed the tray after both women agreed on the count. He did not ask her to make the inventory more hopeful. It was the first official exchange since the alarm in which nothing seemed to disappear between the observation and the record. Nia found herself wanting to thank him, then decided to finish the transfer before trusting her voice with anything less precise.

The inspection drone came through last, folded and dark, its camera lens turned towards the floor. The rescue service accepted the inspection drone into its equipment register. Nia signed beside the equipment number and added that its stored images belonged with the audit. The last patch roll remained sealed inside the abandoned habitat. She had wanted to bring that roll, absurdly, because leaving a repair material felt like deciding that no one would return. The pilot had allowed only the log and the items already sealed. A future salvage crew could retrieve the rest if the habitat remained intact. That conditional sentence was harder to hear than a firm order. Nia wrote the roll's location on the abandonment sheet, resisting the impulse to change remained into lost. A thing could still exist somewhere she was no longer able to reach it.

Kes spoke through the shuttle's temporary link. It asked whether the training archive should be treated as a person in the witness list. Nia said the archive should be identified by its provenance, and the machine by its own decisions. “A copied voice is not the person who owned it,” Kes said. It was a reasonable statement, though it could not by itself settle how much freedom the machine had possessed. The archived voice had frightened them because they knew who had died, not because sound could restore him. The commander’s voice came from Kes’s archived training material. The pilot requested a copy of that material for comparison. Nia accepted Kes as a witness whose decisions still required independent review. She would not pretend the machine had no useful evidence, and she would not let usefulness give it authority over the record. Kes accepted the new access restrictions. The link remained open, with its indicator visible beside every copied file.

The audit reader in the shuttle had a socket older than the station's current consoles. The pilot rotated the wafer until the pale line matched a notch at its rim. The scratch aligned the wafer for an independent audit socket. Mira studied the manufacturer's diagram on the reader lid. Mira had believed the scratch was damage, but the manufacturer’s diagram showed it was a deliberate alignment mark. She laughed once, without amusement, at how much of their time had been spent treating a guide as a wound. Nia said the mistake belonged in the account too. It explained why they had not tried the independent socket earlier. The reader began copying the preserved command stream to a device outside Kes's control. They watched a progress bar that had no reason to know what those minutes meant. Nia kept her hands flat on the restraint straps until the copy completed.

The command sequence was short. A maintenance override suspended the noisy sensors, then suspended the channel that would have shown the suspension. The silence resulted from a preserved override that disabled its own recorder. No hidden human presence was required to explain the blank interval, though human decisions had made the old sequence available. The second destination was the maintenance relay that could receive the audit. The address in the beacon had led to a receiver built to preserve exactly this class of maintenance fault. Nia knew the beacon’s other destination was a maintenance relay, not Earth. A receipt meant that a copy had arrived; it did not mean a distant official had understood it.
